```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.6, dpi = 150)
```

```{r load}
source("R/features.R")
source("R/plotting.R")
x <- readRDS("data/credit.rds")
y <- x$default
f <- build_features(x)
pct <- function(v, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * v)
```

The data are the `r format(nrow(x), big.mark = ",")` credit card holders of a
Taiwanese bank studied by Yeh and Lien (2009). For each client we observe the
credit limit, a few demographic variables and six months of history, April to
September 2005: the repayment status `PAY_t`, the statement balance `BILL_AMT_t`
and the amount paid `PAY_AMT_t`. The target is whether the client defaults in
October 2005; `r pct(mean(y))` do.

Month `t = 1` is September and `t = 6` is April. The source file calls the
September status `PAY_0` and has no `PAY_1`; it is renamed `PAY_1` here so that
the three monthly series share the same index.

`SEX` is dropped from every model. A credit decision may not depend on it, and
leaving it out of the inputs is the minimum; the decision rule is checked for
differences between groups at the end of the project.

## Repayment status codes

The documentation describes `PAY_t = -1` as "paid duly" and `PAY_t = k` for
`k = 1, ..., 9` as a payment delay of `k` months. The values `-2` and `0`, which
make up most of the data, are not documented. The amounts tell what they mean.
For every status, the table gives the share of client-months in which the
previous statement was paid in full and the share in which the current balance
is zero or negative.

```{r codes}
codes <- do.call(rbind, lapply(2:5, function(t) data.frame(
  code = x[[paste0("PAY_", t)]],
  owed = x[[paste0("BILL_AMT", t + 1)]],
  paid = x[[paste0("PAY_AMT", t)]],
  bill = x[[paste0("BILL_AMT", t)]]
)))
codes$group <- ifelse(codes$code >= 1, "1 to 8", as.character(codes$code))
tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(split(codes, codes$group), function(d) data.frame(
  status = d$group[1],
  `client-months` = format(nrow(d), big.mark = ","),
  `previous statement paid in full` = pct(sum(d$paid >= d$owed & d$owed > 0) / sum(d$owed > 0)),
  `balance zero or negative` = pct(mean(d$bill <= 0)),
  check.names = FALSE
)))
tab <- tab[c("-2", "-1", "0", "1 to 8"), ]
knitr::kable(tab, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrr")
```

`-1` is a client who clears the statement, as documented. `-2` is a client with
nothing to pay, either no balance or a balance already settled. `0` is a client
who uses the revolving credit: the statement is not cleared, but the client is
not reported late. The codes are therefore not an ordered scale, and the default rate confirms
it: revolving clients (`0`) default less often than clients who pay in full
(`-1`).

```{r status-plot}
d <- data.frame(code = factor(x$PAY_1), y = y)
d <- aggregate(y ~ code, d, function(v) c(rate = mean(v), n = length(v)))
d <- data.frame(code = d$code, rate = d$y[, "rate"], n = d$y[, "n"])
d <- d[d$n >= 100, ]
ggplot(d, aes(code, rate)) +
  geom_col(fill = ifelse(as.integer(as.character(d$code)) <= 0, palette_main["mid"], palette_main["accent"]),
           width = 0.7) +
  geom_text(aes(label = format(n, big.mark = ",")), vjust = -0.4, size = 3, colour = "grey30") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_axis, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.12))) +
  labs(title = "Default rate by September repayment status",
       subtitle = "Codes with at least 100 clients; labels give the number of clients",
       x = "PAY_1", y = "Default rate in October") +
  theme_report()
```

The code `1` also behaves differently from one month to the next. It is
frequent in September and almost absent before:

```{r code-one}
ones <- sapply(1:6, function(t) sum(x[[paste0("PAY_", t)]] == 1))
knitr::kable(data.frame(t(setNames(format(ones, big.mark = ","), c("Sep", "Aug", "Jul", "Jun", "May", "Apr")))),
             align = "r", row.names = FALSE)
```

In the earlier months a client one month late seems to be recorded as `2` or
not at all. The features below therefore use the number of months late and
whether a client is late at all, rather than the exact code.

## Which statement does a payment settle?

Since `t` counts backwards, the statement of the previous month is
`BILL_AMT_{t+1}`. A payment made in month `t` should settle that statement, not
the one issued at the end of month `t`. The data agree: the
amount paid matches the previous statement exactly far more often than it
matches the current one.

```{r timing}
timing <- data.frame(
  month = c("Sep", "Aug", "Jul", "Jun", "May"),
  `equals previous statement` = sapply(1:5, function(t)
    pct(mean(x[[paste0("PAY_AMT", t)]] == x[[paste0("BILL_AMT", t + 1)]] & x[[paste0("BILL_AMT", t + 1)]] > 0))),
  `equals same-month statement` = sapply(1:5, function(t)
    pct(mean(x[[paste0("PAY_AMT", t)]] == x[[paste0("BILL_AMT", t)]] & x[[paste0("BILL_AMT", t)]] > 0))),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(timing, align = "lrr")
```

Ratios of payment to balance taken within the same month mix two different
statements. All ratios below are aligned.

## Features

Writing $B_t$ for the statement balance, $P_t$ for the amount paid and $L$ for
the credit limit:

| Feature | Definition |
|---|---|
| `status_1`, `delay_1` | September status (no balance, paid in full, revolving, late) and months late |
| `max_delay`, `months_late` | worst delay and number of months late over the six months |
| `months_full`, `months_revolv` | number of months with status `-1` and `0` |
| `worsening` | September delay larger than August delay |
| `util_1`, `util_mean`, `util_slope` | utilisation $u_t = B_t / L$: last value, mean and least-squares trend |
| `repay_1`, `repay_mean` | repayment ratio $r_t = \min(P_t / B_{t+1}, 1)$, set to 1 when $B_{t+1} \le 0$ |
| `nothing_owed_1`, `months_nothing_owed` | $B_{t+1} \le 0$ in September, and the number of such months; separates a client with nothing to pay from one who paid in full, which $r_t$ alone cannot |
| `months_no_pay` | months with $B_{t+1} > 0$ and $P_t = 0$ |
| `spend_1`, `spend_mean` | implied new charges $(B_t - B_{t+1} + P_t) / L$: purchases plus interest and fees |
| `log_limit`, `age`, `education`, `marriage` | as given; undocumented education and marriage codes grouped as `other` |

The charges feature comes from the balance identity
$B_t = B_{t+1} - P_t + \text{purchases}_t + \text{interest and fees}_t$.
Purchases and interest cannot be told apart in the data, so the feature measures
both. It is still the only feature that reacts to what is added to the balance
rather than to what is paid off.

How well does each feature rank clients on its own? The table gives the AUC of
each numeric feature used as a score, oriented so that it is above one half.
This is a description of the full data set, not an out-of-sample result: no
model is fitted, but the same clients will later be split into training and
test sets. Out-of-sample performance is measured in the next part.

```{r univariate}
auc <- function(s) {
  r <- rank(s); n1 <- sum(y); n0 <- length(y) - n1
  a <- (sum(r[y == 1]) - n1 * (n1 + 1) / 2) / (n1 * n0)
  max(a, 1 - a)
}
num <- names(f)[sapply(f, is.numeric)]
same_month <- pmin(ifelse(x$BILL_AMT1 > 0, x$PAY_AMT1 / x$BILL_AMT1, 1), 1)
a <- c(sapply(f[num], auc), `repay_1, same-month statement` = auc(same_month), `PAY_1 as a number` = auc(x$PAY_1))
a <- sort(a, decreasing = TRUE)
knitr::kable(data.frame(feature = names(a), AUC = sprintf("%.3f", a)), row.names = FALSE, align = "lr")
```

The delinquency history dominates, as expected. Counting the months late
(`r sprintf("%.3f", a["months_late"])`) ranks clients better than the raw
September code (`r sprintf("%.3f", a["PAY_1 as a number"])`). Aligning the
repayment ratio with the right statement raises its AUC from
`r sprintf("%.3f", a["repay_1, same-month statement"])` to
`r sprintf("%.3f", a["repay_1"])`.

The `nothing_owed` flags rank clients no better than chance on their own, but
they matter next to the repayment ratio. Among the clients with $r_1 = 1$,
those who had nothing to pay default more often than those who paid the
statement in full:

```{r nothing-owed}
s <- f$repay_1 == 1
no <- data.frame(
  ` ` = c("statement paid in full", "nothing owed"),
  clients = format(as.vector(table(f$nothing_owed_1[s])), big.mark = ","),
  `default rate` = pct(tapply(y[s], f$nothing_owed_1[s], mean)),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(no, align = "lrr", row.names = FALSE)
```

## Spending while not repaying

The expectation was that clients who stop repaying but keep spending, living on
the card, would be the riskiest. The data say otherwise. The two cut-offs below
(10% repaid, new charges above 2% of the limit) were chosen by hand for this
table and are not used anywhere else.

```{r spending}
low_repay <- f$repay_mean < 0.1
spending <- f$spend_mean > 0.02
grp <- data.frame(
  ` ` = c("repays less than 10% on average", "repays more"),
  `no new spending` = c(pct(mean(y[low_repay & !spending])), pct(mean(y[!low_repay & !spending]))),
  `keeps spending` = c(pct(mean(y[low_repay & spending])), pct(mean(y[!low_repay & spending]))),
  check.names = FALSE
)
knitr::kable(grp, align = "lrr")
late <- tapply(f$months_late, interaction(low_repay, spending), mean)
```

The riskiest group repays little and adds little to the balance. These clients
were late in `r sprintf("%.1f", late["TRUE.FALSE"])` of the six months on
average, against `r sprintf("%.1f", late["TRUE.TRUE"])` for those who still
spend. One possible explanation, which the data cannot confirm, is that the bank
restricts the card once a client falls behind; low spending would then follow
from delinquency rather than predict default on its own. The feature is kept for
prediction, but it is not read causally.

## Inputs to the models

Two input sets are compared in the next part.

- **Raw**: the 22 original columns except `SEX`, with the `PAY_t` codes as
  numbers. This is what most analyses of this data set use.
- **Engineered**: the features above.

The features were designed after looking at all 30,000 clients, test clients
included. To keep this from biasing the results, the choice between the two
sets, like every other modelling choice, is made by cross-validation on the
training set only, and the test set is used once at the end. If the engineered
set does not improve the cross-validated log loss, it is not used.
